facts.statehood_note: Entered the Union as a free state after a boundary dispute with Ohio (the Toledo War) was settled; Michigan gave up the Toledo Strip and received the western Upper Peninsula.
facts.nickname: The Great Lakes State (also called the Wolverine State)
facts.motto: Si quaeris peninsulam amoenam circumspice (Latin: If you seek a pleasant peninsula, look about you)
facts.name_origin: Many people say it comes from the Ojibwe word mishigami, meaning 'large water' or 'large lake.' Others connect it to the Mishiiken people of Mackinac Island, as described by Odawa historian Andrew Blackbird.

government.chambers: Michigan Senate (38 members, 4-year terms) and Michigan House of Representatives (110 members, 2-year terms); since 2022, lawmakers may serve 12 years in total
government.executive: Governor (4-year term, limited to two terms). The governor leads the executive branch from the Capitol in Lansing and signs or vetoes bills passed by the Legislature.
government.courts: Michigan Supreme Court (7 justices), the state's court of last resort. Justices are elected to eight-year terms on a nonpartisan ballot; every two years the justices choose one of themselves as chief justice.
government.local: 83 counties, divided into townships (general law and charter townships), plus home-rule cities and villages.
government.constitution: Michigan has had four constitutions (1835, 1850, 1908, and 1963). The current one was approved by voters in 1963 and took effect January 1, 1964.
government.kid_line: "All political power is inherent in the people. Government is instituted for their equal benefit, security and protection." (Article I, Section 1)

long_ago.about: The largest nation in early Michigan, with at least 35,000 people, living in the Upper Peninsula and northern and central Michigan. The Ojibwe, Odawa, and Potawatomi formed the Council of Three Fires.
The Odawa lived mostly south of the Straits of Mackinac in northern, western, and southern Michigan, including the L'Arbre Croche area near today's Harbor Springs.
The Potawatomi lived in southern and western Michigan and nearby parts of Indiana, Illinois, and Wisconsin. They were the third member of the Council of Three Fires.

long_ago.nation: Wendat (Wyandot; called Huron by the French)
long_ago.about: An Iroquoian-speaking people who had a village near the Detroit River, close to where the French built Detroit.

first_peoples.today_note: Michigan has 12 federally recognized tribes. Besides those listed here, they are the Hannahville Indian Community, the Lac Vieux Desert Band of Lake Superior Chippewa Indians, the Little River Band of Ottawa Indians, and the Gun Lake Tribe (Match-e-be-nash-she-wish Band of Pottawatomi Indians).

history.event: Native peoples on the Keweenaw Peninsula begin mining and using copper.
Men from French explorer Étienne Brûlé's expedition become the first Europeans to reach what is now Michigan.
Father Jacques Marquette starts a Catholic mission at Sault Ste. Marie, the first permanent European settlement in Michigan.
Antoine de la Mothe Cadillac founds Fort Pontchartrain du Détroit on the Detroit River; it grows into a fur-trading town near a Wyandot village.
Odawa leader Pontiac and warriors from many nations rise up against British rule after the French and Indian War, including a siege of Fort Detroit.
Under the Jay Treaty, Britain finally leaves Detroit and Michilimackinac to the United States.
In the War of 1812, the U.S. general William Hull surrenders Detroit to the British; Americans retake it in September 1813.
Laura Smith Haviland's family farm in Lenawee County becomes the first Underground Railroad station in Michigan.
In the Treaty of Washington, Odawa and Ojibwe (Chippewa) leaders give up about 37 percent of Michigan's land to the United States, after earlier treaties in 1819 and 1821 took other lands.
On January 26, Michigan becomes the 26th state, entering the Union as a free state.
'Copper fever' brings one of the first mining rushes in the United States to the Keweenaw Peninsula.
The 1st Michigan Colored Infantry, 845 men from Detroit, southern Michigan, and Canada, some of them freedom seekers, is mustered on February 17 and later becomes the 102nd U.S. Colored Infantry.
During Reconstruction, Sojourner Truth, living in Battle Creek, tries to vote on Election Day but is turned away.

trailblazers.name: Sojourner Truth
trailblazers.text: Born into slavery in New York, she escaped to freedom in 1826 and became a famous speaker for abolition and women's rights. She moved to Michigan in 1857 and lived in Battle Creek until her death; after the Civil War she worked for seven years to win land for formerly enslaved people.

trailblazers.name: Laura Smith Haviland
trailblazers.text: She and her husband started the Raisin Institute school in 1837, and their farm became Michigan's first Underground Railroad station. She hid freedom seekers, sometimes guided them to Canada herself, and later worked for women's voting rights.

trailblazers.name: Andrew J. Blackbird (Makade-binesi)
trailblazers.text: Born in the L'Arbre Croche area (now Harbor Springs), he served as an interpreter and became a historian. In 1887 he published a book on the history of the Odawa (Ottawa) and Ojibwe (Chippewa) people of Michigan, telling his people's history in his own words.

trailblazers.name: Elijah McCoy
trailblazers.text: Born in Ontario to parents who had escaped slavery in Kentucky through the Underground Railroad, he grew up in Ypsilanti and trained as a mechanical engineer in Scotland. In 1872 he earned his first patent, for an automatic lubricator (oil-drip cup) for steam engines, and by his death he held more than 50 U.S. patents. In 2012 the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office named its first regional office, in Detroit, for him.

trailblazers.name: George DeBaptiste
trailblazers.text: Born free in Virginia, he moved to Detroit in 1846 and was called the 'president' of its Underground Railroad group. He bought a lake steamboat to carry freedom seekers across the Detroit River to Canada, and with William Lambert helped hundreds reach freedom. After the Civil War he helped Black children gain admission to Detroit public schools.

trailblazers.name: Grace Lee Boggs
trailblazers.text: The daughter of Chinese immigrants, she moved to Detroit with her husband James Boggs and spent decades working for civil rights and stronger neighborhoods. She helped found the Detroit Asian Political Alliance in 1970 and wrote books into her 90s.

geography.regions: Two peninsulas joined by the Mackinac Bridge: the heavily forested, more mountainous Upper Peninsula and the flatter, more populated Lower Peninsula, both shaped by glaciers and nearly surrounded by the Great Lakes.

ecosystems.name: Great Lakes sand dunes
ecosystems.about: At Sleeping Bear Dunes, bluffs tower 450 feet above Lake Michigan, and endangered Great Lakes piping plovers nest on the beaches.

ecosystems.name: Northern forests
ecosystems.about: The Upper Peninsula is heavily forested, and Sleeping Bear Dunes alone has more than 50 mammal species, including black bears and river otters.

ecosystems.name: Isle Royale island wilderness
ecosystems.about: On Isle Royale in Lake Superior, gray wolves hunt moose; wolves likely reached the island over an ice bridge in the winter of 1948.

science.weather: Hot or warm summers and cold winters, colder in the north. Heavy lake-effect snow falls in winter, and some northern areas get almost 160 inches of snow a year. The state averages 17 tornadoes a year, mostly in the far south, plus about 30 days of thunderstorms.
science.resources: Copper, iron, and lumber built early Michigan; the state led the nation in lumber from the 1850s to the 1880s. Today Detroit is the center of the U.S. auto industry, and the state also has manufacturing, farming, forestry, tourism, and high-tech jobs.
science.highlight: Isle Royale National Park in Lake Superior is famous for its wolves and moose: when moose are plentiful, wolves do well, and wolves keep the moose herd healthy by hunting old, young, and sick animals.
